column2: and the qualities of the mind likewise, and the qualities of space, and the qualities of wind, righteous-souled one, and again the qualities of light,
the qualities of water, Partha, and the qualities of earth too: the knower of the field, Yudhishthira, pervades them all with qualities by his whole self.
The self goes to the knower of the field, and so do deeds good and bad, and the senses, lord, like pupils to the great soul.
Passing beyond nature too, he goes to the imperishable self, the supreme Narayana-self, beyond the pairs, beyond nature.
Freed from merit and sin, having entered the free of disease, the Supreme Self without qualities, he does not return, Bharata.
What remains here, dear, is the mind and the senses, which come in due time, obeying the teacher's command.
In a short time peace can be reached by the seeker of virtue; so, Kaunteya, by one joined, with joined knowledge, seeking liberation.
The Sankhyas, king, greatly wise, go to the highest goal; there is no knowledge equal to this knowledge, Kaunteya.
Let there be no doubt in you here: Sankhya knowledge is held supreme: the imperishable, firm, unmanifest, the first eternal Brahman,
without beginning, middle or end, beyond the pairs, the doer, eternal, unchanging and constant, which the peaceful speak of,
from which all the modifications of creation and dissolution go on, and which they proclaim in the scriptures and the great sages declare.
All brahmanas and gods and people who know tradition speak of the supreme god, devoted to brahmanas, endless, beyond, imperishable.
The great knowledge that is among the great, king, in the Vedas, in Sankhya, and likewise in yoga, and whatever varied ancient lore is seen, all of it, lord of men, has come from Sankhya.

What is seen in the great histories, and in the science of wealth cherished by the refined, king, and whatever knowledge there is in the world here, that great thing, great soul, has come from Sankhya.
Peace is seen, and supreme strength, and subtle knowledge rightly told, austerities and subtle pleasures: all are rightly laid down in Sankhya, king.
In the reverse of it, Partha, the Sankhyas ever go happily to the gods, and having moved them, their purpose done, they fall again among striving brahmins.

Leaving the body, the Sankhyas enter liberation, Partha, like the dwellers in heaven into the sky; therefore the twice-born delight more in Sankhya, so worthy, loved by the refined, lord of the earth.
For them no animal birth is seen, no downward goal, no dwelling of sinners; nor are those twice-born unwise who are devoted to this knowledge, lord of men.
Sankhya is vast, supreme, ancient, a spotless great ocean, noble and lovely; the great soul Narayana, king, holds the whole Sankhya, immeasurable.
This truth has been told by me, king; Narayana is this ancient universe; at creation he makes creation, and at dissolution he devours it again."
[Yudhishthira said:] "I wish to understand the manifestation of the imperishable and the perishable, slayer of foes, mighty-armed, delight of the Kurus, in truth.
For you are called a treasury of knowledge by brahmanas who master the Veda, and by greatly fortunate sages and great-souled ascetics.
Few days remain to you, with the sun in its southern course; when the blessed sun has turned, you will go to the highest goal.
When you have gone, from whom shall we hear the good? You are the lamp of the Kuru line, shining with the wealth of knowledge.
I wish to hear this from you, bull of the Kuru line; I am not sated, king of kings, hearing such nectar."
[Bhishma said:] "Here I shall relate to you an ancient tale, the dialogue of Vasishtha and Karala Janaka.
Janaka the king asked Vasishtha, the best of sages, shining like the sun, seated, about the supreme knowledge of the highest good.
Having saluted with folded hands the son of Mitra and Varuna, seated, skilled in the supreme self-knowledge and settled in the course of the self:
Know an age as twelve thousand; an aeon is four times that; repeated ten hundred times, that is called Brahma's day, and the night is as long, king, at whose end he awakes.

He creates the great being of endless action, the eldest being, the embodied one, formless in self, the universe of the Self-born; Shambhu, with minuteness, lightness and attainment, the lord, the imperishable light.
He has hands and feet everywhere, eyes, heads and faces everywhere, ears everywhere in the world; he stands covering all.
This blessed Hiranyagarbha is called intellect; in the yogas he is also called Mahat and Virinchi.
In Sankhya doctrine he is read by many names, of manifold nature, of varied form, the self of the universe, called the one syllable.
Because by himself he covers the whole three worlds, not of one self, and because of his many forms, he is called Vishvarupa.
This one, changed, creates himself by himself: ego, of great energy, and the Prajapati made of ego.
From the unmanifest the manifest arises; they call it the creation of knowledge; the great and ego too are the creation of ignorance.
Non-rule and rule arose together, called by the thinkers on scripture and shastra knowledge and ignorance.
Know the creation of elements from ego as the third, lord of the earth; and know the changed one, the fourth, among elements in ego.
Wind, light, space, water and earth, and sound, touch, form, taste and smell,
thus arisen together, the tenfold group, without doubt; know, king of kings, the elemental creation as the fifth, with meaning.
Ear, skin, eyes, tongue and nose as fifth; speech, hands, feet, anus and genital;
these are the senses of knowledge and the senses of action, arisen here together with the mind, lord of the earth.
This twenty-four-fold set of principles operates in all forms; knowing it, the brahmanas who see the truth do not grieve.
This is said of the body in all embodied beings in the three worlds, best of men, among gods, men and Danavas,
with yakshas, beings, gandharvas, kinnaras and great serpents, with charanas and pishachas, with divine sages and night-roamers,
with gnats, worms and mosquitoes, with putrid worms and mice, in dog and dog-eater, in the sons of Vinata, with chandalas and pulkasas,
in elephants, horses, asses and tigers, in trees and cows: whatever is made of form, this is the illustration everywhere.
In water, on earth and in space, not elsewhere: so it is settled; the embodied have a place: so we have heard.
All this, dear, called the manifest, flows away; day by day the self of beings flows; therefore it is called perishable.
This is called the imperishable; as the world flows, they call the world delusive; they call the unmanifest the manifest by name.
And the Great, the eldest, is ever the illustration of the perishable; I have told you that, great king, from which one does not return.
The twenty-fifth is Vishnu, without principle, called the principle; through reliance on the principles the wise call this the principle.
What the formless created as manifest, the formless one rests in as form; the twenty-fourth is manifest, but the twenty-fifth is formless.
He alone, self-possessed, abides in the heart of all forms, conscious, making conscious, eternal, the form of all and the formless.
Of the nature of non-creation and non-dissolution, though the law of creation and dissolution is of nature, he is ever in the sphere, without qualities, called by qualities.
Thus this great self, knowing creation and dissolution, modifying, joined with nature, thinks himself, unawake.
Joined with tamas, sattva and rajas, he is dissolved in these and those wombs here, from being unawakened, from serving the unawake.
By dwelling together he thinks, as dweller, "I am not another"; saying "who I am, he I am," he turns after the qualities.
By tamas he reaches the manifold tamasic states, by rajas the rajasic, and by relying on sattva the sattvic.
White, red and black: these three forms; know all these forms to be of nature.
The tamasic go to hell, the rajasic to men, the sattvic go to the world of the gods, sharers of happiness.
By unmixed sin he would gain an animal womb; by merit and sin, humanity; by merit alone, divinity.
Thus the wise call the perishable the object of the unmanifest; this twenty-fifth proceeds from knowledge alone."
[Vasishtha said:] "In thousands of animal wombs, sometimes even among the gods, he is born by union with the qualities, by the destruction of qualities.
From humanity he goes to heaven, from heaven to humanity, from humanity to a place in hell, and reaches the endless.
As the silkworm binds itself with the qualities of the silk thread, so this one without qualities is bound by qualities.
Beyond the pairs, he meets the pairs in these and those wombs here: in headache, eye disease, toothache, throat ailments,
dropsy, piles, fever, boils, cholera, leucoderma, leprosy, burning, skin disease, epilepsy and forgetfulness;
and whatever other varied common pairs arise in embodied beings, he thinks these his; and likewise, through self-conceit, he thinks his good deeds.
One-clothed, ill-clothed, always sleeping on the ground, sleeping like a frog, and in the hero's posture,
wearing bark, sleeping and standing in the open, on a bed of bricks and on a bed of thorns,
on various beds, with the unfruited greedy for fruit, wearing munja girdle, nakedness, linen and black antelope skins,
hemp, hair garment, tiger-skin covering, lion-skin garment, and silk garments,
tree-bark clothing and garments of rags: many other garments, the unwise thinks.
Varied foods and various jewels; living on one cloth's edge; eating once a day;
eating every fourth meal-time, or at the sixth meal-time, or eating at night, or eating every eighth day,
living seven nights, ten days, or twelve days without food, fasting a month, living on roots, living on fruit,
feeding on wind, water, oil-cake, cow dung, cow urine, vegetables and flowers,
eating moss, living on rinsing water, living on withered leaves, eating scattered fruit,
he undergoes various austerities in desire for happiness, the Chandrayanas by rule and various marks,
he resorts to the path of the four stages and the stages, and attends heresies, caves and mountains,
solitary places, shade of rocks, springs, various mutterings and various vows,
rules of many kinds, various austerities, sacrifices of many forms and various rites,
the path of trade, brahmins, kshatriyas, vaishyas and shudras, and gifts of many forms even to the poor, blind and wretched,
he thinks, from lack of awakening, the three kinds of qualities, sattva, rajas and tamas, dharma, wealth and desire; the self thus divides itself by nature.
Svadha, vashat, svaha, salutation, officiating, teaching, giving, they say receiving, sacrifice and study, and whatever else,
in the dispute of birth and death, and in slaughter: all this, they say, is the path of action, made of good and bad.
The goddess Nature makes even the great dissolution; at the end of the day, the one remains, having reached these qualities.
As the sun withdraws the net of rays in time, so this one repeatedly thinks all as play.
These various qualities of the form of the self, dear to the heart, thus modifying, he does the works of creation and dissolution.
Attached to the path of action and non-action, threefold in qualities and beyond the three, joined to the path of action and non-action, he thinks "this is that."
Thus these pairs go on in me always; they are born from me alone, and they afflict me: so he thinks.
All these are to be crossed, lord of men, he thinks, from lack of awakening, and so his good deeds.
These are to be enjoyed by me, gone to the world of the gods; here itself I shall enjoy the rise of fruit of good and bad.

Happiness alone is to be done; having done it once, happiness will be mine; and as long as my happiness lasts, it will come in birth after birth.
mahabharata:12:292.35	And sorrow will be mine, endless, by what is done here; human life is great sorrow, and sinking in hell.
mahabharata:12:292.36	From hell, too, I shall in time come to humanity again; from humanity to divinity, from divinity to manhood again; from humanity he goes in turn to hell.
He who ever knows thus, covered with the qualities of the self without self, is born by that in gods, men and hell.
Covered by the sense of mine, he turns about in just that, through thousands of crores of creations, in forms ending in death.
He who does action whose nature is good and bad fruit himself enjoys the fruit in the three worlds, embodied.
Nature does action whose nature is good and bad fruit; and nature enjoys it in the three worlds, moving at will.
In animal wombs, in humanity and in the world of the gods: know these three places to be of nature.
They call nature markless; we infer it by marks; so he sees the human mark by inference.
Having reached another mark, the unwounded mark of nature, resting on the doors of wounds, he thinks actions in the self.
Hearing and the rest, and the five senses of action, speech and the rest, go on in the qualities alone, with qualities; "I do these," "these senses are mine."
The senseless thinks, "I have wounds; I am unwounded"; the markless thinks the mark is the self, the timeless thinks time is the self.
The one without goodness thinks goodness is the self, the one without principle thinks principle is the self, the deathless thinks death is the self, the unmoving thinks the moving is the self.
The one without field thinks the field is the self, without creation thinks creation is the self, without austerity thinks austerity is the self, without goal thinks goal is the self.
The unborn thinks birth is the self, the fearless thinks fear is the self, the imperishable thinks the perishable is the self, the unawake thinks so."
[Vasishtha said:] "By power he goes to thousands of powers, ending in death, in animal wombs, in humanity, and likewise in the world of the gods.
Like the moon from its stores, again there thousands of times, he dissolves from not being awakened; thus is the unwise.
The fifteen parts are the womb, called the power; know it as constant, and Soma as the sixteenth part.
The unwise is born again and again in a part constantly; they use its power, and again he is born.
The sixteenth part is subtle; understand that as Soma; it is not used by the gods; it joins the gods.
Having wasted it so, best of kings, he is born; that is seen as his nature; by its waning, liberation is said.
Thus the body of sixteen parts, called unmanifest, thinking "this is mine," turns about in just that.
And the twenty-fifth is the self, from not being awakened to that; of the stainless and purified by the practice of the pure wind.
The unpure becomes the pure-souled of that kind, lord of the earth; and from serving the unawake, even the awake goes to unawakeness.
Likewise one not awakened should be known, best of kings: by serving the threefold nature, he would become of nature."
[Karala Janaka said:] "This relation of the imperishable and the perishable is held to be as between woman and man, blessed one; the relation is spoken of so.
Without a man a woman does not bear a child here; without a woman a man would not produce a form.
By mutual union, by resting on each other's qualities, the form is produced; so it is in all wombs.
For delight, by mutual restraint, resting on each other's qualities, the form is produced in the season; I shall tell the illustration.
The qualities of the man here and those of the mother, bone, sinew and marrow, we know are from the father, twice-born.
Skin, flesh and blood we have heard are from the mother; thus, best of the twice-born, it is read in the Vedic shastras.
What is the authority said by the Veda and read in the shastras: the authority of Veda and shastra is the eternal authority.
Thus nature and the Person are ever bound together; I see, blessed one, therefore that there is no dharma of liberation.
Now another illustration immediately follows: tell it to me truly, for you are in every way direct.
We too, desiring liberation, wish for what is free of disease, bodiless, ageless, divine, beyond the senses, without master."
[Vasishtha said:] "What you have said, citing Veda and shastra, is so; but you do not grasp it as it is.
The text of both Veda and shastra is borne by you, but you are not rightly a knower of the truth of the text, lord of men.
He who is intent on bearing the text of Veda and shastra and does not know the truth of the meaning of the text, his bearing it is vain.
He carries the load of that text who does not know its meaning; but one who knows the truth of the meaning has not learned the text in vain.
Asked the meaning of a text, such a one can tell; he finds its meaning by approaching the truth as it is.
But the dull-witted who tells the meaning of a text in assemblies, how will he of slow understanding tell the text by determination?
The hole-minded one will not tell the determination in truth; he comes to be laughed at, though self-possessed.
Therefore hear, king of kings, how this is seen in truth in the Sankhyas and in the yogas, among great souls.
What yogis see is followed by the Sankhyas; he who sees Sankhya and yoga as one is wise.
Skin, flesh, blood, fat, bile, marrow, bone and sinew: this is of the senses, dear, which you have spoken of.
From substance the origin of substance, from sense a sense, from body a body, and from seed seed.
For the senseless, seedless, substanceless embodied one, how will qualities arise, since the great soul is without qualities?
Qualities arise in qualities and enter there; thus qualities arise from nature and are not.
Skin, flesh, blood, fat, bile, marrow, bone and sinew, with semen as eighth: know these as of nature.
Man and not-man: the threefold mark is of nature; he is neither man nor not-man; he is called the possessor of marks.
Markless nature is perceived by its marks born of itself, as the seasons are always perceived by flowers and fruits as their forms.
So by inference the markless is perceived; the twenty-fifth, dear, is of unfixed nature among marks.
Without beginning or end, endless, all-seeing, free of disease; by mere conceit he is said to have no quality among qualities.
Qualities belong to one with qualities; how for one without quality? So those who see qualities know.
But when this one thinks all these qualities of nature are his, then he, though endowed with qualities, sees by the supreme.
What is beyond intellect, the Sankhyas and yogis all say, the greatly wise one who is awake, by the avoidance of the unawake.
The unawakened unmanifest they call the lord with qualities, and the lord without qualities, eternal, and the overseer.
The wise skilled in Sankhya and yoga who seek the highest understand the twenty-fifth of nature and the qualities.
When the awakened, fearing the birth of the unmanifest state, awaken the one awakening, then they bring him to equality.
This illustration is right and the wrong view; of the awake and unawake it is separately, scourge of foes.
Of each other, this illustration of the perishable and imperishable is told: they call oneness imperishable and manyness perishable.
When this one who stands in the twenty-fifth proceeds rightly, his seeing is oneness and his non-seeing is manyness.
This is a distinct illustration of the principled and the unprincipled; the wise call the creation of twenty-five the principle.
They call the unprincipled the supreme illustration of the twenty-fifth; the group of the group, conduct, the principle, eternal from the principle."
[Karala Janaka said:] "Thus, sinless one, for one awakening through the unawake and the awake, with dull understanding I do not see this truth; there is no doubt.
The reason you told for the imperishable and perishable, even that, sinless one, has as if been lost by my unsteady understanding.
I wish to hear this view of oneness and manyness, the awake, the unawake and the awakening one, in truth.
Knowledge and ignorance, blessed one, the imperishable and the perishable, Sankhya and yoga, wholly, both separate and not separate."
[Vasishtha said:] "Well, I shall tell you what you ask; hear the duty of yoga separately, great king.
The duty of yoga for the yogas is meditation, the supreme strength; the Veda-knowers say that meditation is of two kinds.
One-pointedness of the mind and control of breath; and the control of breath is with quality, and the mind's without quality.
At voiding urine, excrement and at eating, lord of men, he should not engage at the three times; he should join the rest intent.
By them the self is always to be known: so we have heard; substance is for the one of undiminished mind, not otherwise: so it is settled.
Freed from all attachments, light of diet, master of senses, he should hold the mind in the self in the early and late night.
Having steadied the host of senses by the mind, lord of Mithila, and made the mind steady by intellect, unmoving like a stone,
he should be unshaken like a post and motionless like a mountain; the wise who know the rule's provision call that then joined.
He does not hear, smell, taste or see, and does not know touch; the mind does not intend.
He thinks of nothing, he is not aware, like wood; then the wise call him joined, come to nature.
As a lamp burning in a windless place is seen, so he, motionless and unmoving, would not take a course upward or crosswise.
Then he should see him, in whom, when seen, it is said the "inner self in the heart," the knower, to be known, dear, by those like me.
Like smokeless fire, like the sun with rays, like lightning in the sky, the self is seen in the self.
Whom the great-souled, steadfast, wise brahmanas, established in the womb of Brahman, see as the wombless, of immortal nature.
That, they say, is smaller than the small, greater than the great; within all beings it stands firm and is not seen.
He is seen by the substance of intellect and by the lamp of mind, maker of the world; standing beyond great darkness, free of tamas, dear.
He is called the darkness-dispeller by the knowers of truth who have mastered the Veda, stainless, free of darkness, markless, called markless.
This yoga of the yogas I hold the mark of yoga; thus seeing, they see the self, ageless and supreme.
The vision of yoga has been told to you by me in truth; I shall tell the knowledge of Sankhya, the illustration of enumeration.
The speakers of nature call the unmanifest the supreme nature; from it the great is born, second, best of kings.
We have heard that ego is the third from the great; the Sankhya illustrators say the five elements come from ego.
These are the eight natures, and the sixteen modifications, and the five particular ones, and the five senses.
So many principles alone the wise call Sankhya; the Sankhyas, knowing the rule's provision, are ever devoted to the path of Sankhya.
From whatever a thing is born, it dissolves in that; they dissolve in reverse and are created by the inner self.
They are born in direct order and dissolve in reverse; qualities constantly in qualities, like the waves of the ocean.
So much is the complete dissolution of nature, best of kings; its oneness at dissolution and manyness when it creates; so, king of kings, it should be known by thinkers on the knowable.
The unmanifest has an overseer; this is its illustration; the oneness and manyness of nature follow the principles; its oneness is at dissolution and manyness at activity.
The self would make nature in many forms, of the nature of production; that field the great self, the twenty-fifth, presides over.
Overseer is the word the best ascetics use, king; from presiding he is the overseer of the fields: so we have heard.
He knows the field and the unmanifest and is called the knower of the field; he lies in the unmanifest city and is called Purusha.
The field is one thing and the knower of the field another; the field is called the unmanifest, and the knower is the twenty-fifth.
Knowledge is one thing and the knowable another; knowledge is called the unmanifest, and the knowable is the twenty-fifth.
The unmanifest is called the field, and so is sattva, and the lord; the non-lord, the unprincipled and the principle is the twenty-fifth.
This much is the vision of Sankhya, the vision of enumeration; it makes Sankhya and they call it nature.
The Sankhyas, having enumerated the twenty-four principles in truth, with nature, the twenty-fifth is without principle.
The twenty-fifth is called the unawakened self when awakening; when he awakens to the self he becomes alone.
This much right vision has been told to you in truth; those who know thus reach equality.
The right illustration is called direct, and so of nature; these are the qualities and principles; the other would be without qualities."
Hearing the words of the Brahman-speakers, the wise king, reaching supreme joy, said, "So be it."
Thus addressed by the king of the gods, Kauravya, Brihaspati, after thinking a moment, said to the king of the gods:
[Yudhishthira said:] "He whose strength is that of ten thousand elephants, this king, having taken refuge with a woman, lies like one lifeless."
I shall practise austerity; learn that from me. Going to the forest with Rama. Having said this, Krishna touched his father's feet with his head and quickly left.
Bathing here, your human state will leave you; you will be free of grief and effort, with enmity gone.
